A SEA OF TRASH FLOODS THE RIVER BESIDE BACLARAN CHURCH A massive accumulation of garbage from Manila Bay filled the river in front of Baclaran Church in Parañaque City on Monday, August 10, as heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon or Habagat swept debris into the area. The thick layer of floating waste created an alarming scene, with trash covering a large portion of the waterway. Nearby residents said they had never experienced anything like this before, highlighting the unusual scale of the debris buildup following the heavy rainfall. The incident once again raises concerns about waste management, waterways, and the impact of heavy rains on communities near Manila Bay. WAIST-DEEP FLOODWATERS IN KAWIT, CAVITE Residents were forced to wade through chest-deep floodwaters along Toclong-San Sebastian Road and Tramo Street in Barangay Gahak, Kawit, Cavite after a nearby river overflowed amid continuous monsoon rains on August 8, 2026. Residents said flooding has become a recurring problem whenever heavy rains hit the area, raising concerns over the river’s capacity to carry water during prolonged rainfall. Some residents also pointed to structures along the river, which they believe may be obstructing the natural flow of water and contributing to the flooding. They are calling on authorities to conduct an inspection of the river and surrounding structures, identify possible obstructions, and take appropriate measures to help prevent or reduce flooding in the community. As heavy rains continue, residents are urged to remain alert, avoid wading through floodwaters whenever possible, and follow advisories from local authorities.  Photos by Rene H. METRO MANILA FACES SEVERE INUNDATION DESPITE PREVIOUS DISASTER FOCUS ON MINDANAO Netizens Contrast NCR Flood Crisis with Normal Daily Life in Davao City Following Palace Statements MANILA, Philippines — Heavy downpours have left vast portions of Metro Manila submerged, sparking renewed public discussion over recent statements by Presidential Communications Office Undersecretary Castro regarding regional flood vulnerabilities. Earlier comments from Usec. Castro highlighted Davao as a primary center for flooding concerns in the country. However, current conditions show the National Capital Region bearing the brunt of severe waterlogging, causing major traffic disruptions and stranded commuters across key thoroughfares. Meanwhile, viral footage and social media posts show residents in Davao City enjoying routine outdoor activities, including community basketball games, under manageable weather conditions. Local authorities in Metro Manila are currently deploying emergency teams and pumps to clear inundated avenues, while disaster management officials reiterate that flood monitoring remains active nationwide regardless of shifting weather patterns. #1DNews | Davao, Philippines  FLOOD ALERT | Street Flooding Hits Carmelite Area in Bajada Following Hours of Rain LOOK: Residents of the Carmelite area in Bajada, Davao City, experienced street flooding early Wednesday, July 1, after several hours of continuous rainfall overnight. According to residents, flooding in the area is a recurring problem whenever heavy rains persist for more than two hours. As of this morning, floodwaters had reportedly risen from knee to waist level in some sections, affecting road access and threatening nearby homes, vehicles, and other properties. While residents noted that floodwaters typically recede within two to three hours after the rain stops, many continue to express concern over the recurring flooding and the damage it brings to their belongings and daily activities. Authorities are advising motorists and the public to exercise caution when passing through flood-prone areas. FOR THE NATION, NOT FOR DRAMA To our public servants in Congress: We don't need your tears. We need your receipts. The ₱7.2-trillion budget for 2027 belongs to every Filipino. It belongs to the farmer in Nueva Ecija, the fisherman in Samar, the OFW in Dubai, the jeepney driver in Cebu, and the teacher in Mindanao. It came from our taxes, our sweat, and our sacrifices. So instead of crying in the session hall, hold a press conference and tell the people:  "We approved your budget."  "Here is where every peso goes."  "Here is what your city and province will receive."  "We are ready to serve you in 2027." The House passed the ₱7.2-trillion budget on second reading on October 7, with ₱116 billion in amendments, and the final vote is set for Monday, October 12. Budget watchdogs are already warning that about ₱541.4 billion could go to "pork allocations". That is why the Filipino people are asking: WHERE IS THE MONEY GOING?  DPWH: ₱644 billion. Which roads, bridges and flood controls? Where, and when will they be finished?  Agriculture and agrarian reform: ₱276.57 billion. Will it reach our farmers?  DSWD: ₱241.56 billion. Will it reach the families who need it most? Our call is simple. POST THE BUDGET in every city hall, every provincial capitol and every barangay. Put it online, line by line, project by project. Let every Filipino see, check and monitor where the money goes. Transparency is not a favor. It is our right. Accountability is not optional. It is your duty. We don't pay taxes for tears. We pay for roads, schools, hospitals, jobs and our future. The people's money is for the people.  #Budget2027 #PeopleMoney #TransparencyNow #AccountabilityNow #ForTheNation #ProudFilipino See less FOR THE NATION, NOT FOR DRAMA

DAVAO: THE “FLOOD CAPITAL” — BUT PERHAPS NOT FOR THE REASON YOU THINK They say Davao is the “Flood Capital of the Philippines.” Well, if someone insists on giving us that crown, perhaps we should wear it proudly—but let’s first ask a simple question: What exactly is overflowing?  Yes, Davao experiences floods. We have rivers that swell after relentless rain, low-lying communities that sometimes bear the brunt of nature, sudden downpours that seem to arrive without an appointment, and roads that occasionally transform into temporary swimming pools. That is a real problem. It deserves real solutions—not political theater. But if we are going to compare cities, perhaps the scoreboard deserves more than a political slogan. During the severe southwest monsoon flooding in July 2025, for example, the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority reported hundreds of flooding incidents across Metro Manila within a single day. So before anyone points a finger at Davao, perhaps we should remember that flooding is not a problem exclusive to one city. Water does not check political affiliations before it rises. Rain does not ask who you voted for before it pours. And rivers certainly don't read campaign speeches.  But here's where I see Davao differently. Because there is another kind of flooding happening here—one that doesn't destroy homes, close roads, or leave mud behind. Davao floods with culture. Walk through this city and you encounter a living mosaic of Mindanao: Indigenous traditions, migrant communities, different languages, cuisines, beliefs, stories, and histories woven together into one constantly evolving urban tapestry. Ask someone where they came from, and you may discover an entire story behind the answer. Then, inevitably, there's food. Because in Davao, you can start a conversation about almost anything and somehow end up discussing durian.  “This variety is sweeter.” “No, that one has better texture.” “You haven't tried the best one yet.” Suddenly, what began as a casual conversation has transformed into an international conference on durian. No registration fee required.  But perhaps Davao's most remarkable flood is neither water nor culture. It is warmth. There is a quiet generosity in the character of many Dabawenyos that statistics cannot measure. You can arrive as a stranger and, before long, someone may already be telling you where to eat, what places to visit, which shortcut to take—and, most importantly, which road to avoid when traffic is terrible. That's not just hospitality. That's hospitality with a built-in traffic advisory.  And then there is Davao's natural beauty. The sea. Samal. Mount Apo. The forests. The farms. The rivers. The mountains. The wide spaces that remind you that progress and nature do not always have to be enemies. Davao is also changing. Businesses are arriving. Buildings are rising. Infrastructure is expanding. Communities are growing. People continue to come—not only because they are looking for jobs, but because they are looking for possibilities. Some arrive carrying résumés. Others arrive carrying business plans. Some arrive carrying nothing more than a dream. And somewhere along the way, many discover something unexpected: They don't merely live in Davao. They become part of it. That, perhaps, is the real story. A city should not be judged solely by the problems that rise within it. It should also be judged by what its people continue to build despite those problems. Davao is not perfect. We have traffic. We have growing pains. We have environmental concerns. We have infrastructure challenges. We have political disagreements. And, of course, we have social-media experts who can apparently repair the entire country using nothing but a smartphone and a Facebook account.  But beneath all the noise is something far more difficult to construct: Character. You can build a highway. You can build skyscrapers. You can build malls, bridges, offices, and massive developments. You can even build a spectacular roundabout that everyone will complain about for months.  But you cannot manufacture belonging. You cannot pour it into concrete. You cannot buy it from a catalog. It has to grow. And Davao has grown through people. People from different places came here. They planted roots. They built families. They opened businesses. They raised children. They created communities. And little by little, their individual stories became part of the larger story of the city. For the past 15 years, I have had the privilege of traveling around Davao for team-building activities, retreats, seminars, workshops, and speaking engagements. And in those years, I have seen something that no flood statistics can capture. I have seen people flood others with smiles, generosity, and warmth. So if someone wants to call Davao the “Flood Capital of the Philippines,” perhaps we shouldn't be offended. Maybe we should simply redefine the flood. NBI Serves Subpoena to DPWH Davao Director Amid Flood Control Probe DAVAO CITY— The National Bureau of Investigation has served a subpoena to DPWH Davao Regional Director Juby Blancaver Cordon as part of its ongoing investigation into alleged anomalies in flood control projects in Davao Region. The subpoena was issued as the NBI looks into reports of irregularities and questionable disbursements tied to flood mitigation works in the area. Investigators said Cordon was required to appear before the bureau and submit documents related to project implementation, bidding, and fund utilization. The probe forms part of a wider scrutiny of flood control spending nationwide following public complaints and reports of substandard or incomplete projects despite large budget allocations.

Polk County Weather Update | 11:45 P.M. Hurricane Isaias made landfall along the Gulf Coast earlier this evening and continues to move inland. We will provide updates, warning information, and local impact reports as conditions warrant throughout the overnight hours and into the weekend.

text: Please SHARE:    GEORGIA 7 PM FRIDAY UPDATE: Isaias is making landfall right now on the Florida Gulf Coast as a category 3 major hurricane. Not a good night in places like Fort Walton, 30A, Destin, Navarre, Miramar, and Pensacola Beaches.  We have most of the area in a HIGH WIND WARNING beginning overnight tonight for wind gusts of 30-50 mph, with a couple stronger than that. A TROPICAL STORM WARNING continues for a couple of our counties to the southwest. Tornado warnings could start overnight tonight with most coming tomorrow. Make sure you have a way to receive severe weather alerts. A lot of times when we talk about tropical tornadoes, they are weak and short-lived. But, we *cannot* make that promise this time. One or two strong tornadoes could be in the picture.  LATEST TIMELINE: Rain to spreading from south to north across Metro Atlanta and North Georgia right now (7 PM). It will be widespread and heavy at times, at first. The map with arrival time of tropical storm force winds is attached in the post.  By 7-9 AM, the shower activity will be a little more broken a part, in a traditional tropical squall sense. These will last through the day and as the day wears on, elevate the tornado threat. With daylight comes more instability for these to work with (thus the tornado threat continuing). I expect this to peak across eastern Georgia in the mid-to-late afternoon.  These tropical squalls will linger into the evening. They will begin to taper off as the sun sets Saturday night, with only a handful left by Sunday morning. Yes, this will be a long-duration event.  THREATS  WIND: The forecast has ticked up a bit for the wind gusts. I'm becoming more convinced that we'll see more 50+ mph gusts than initially thought. Widespread 40-60 mph gusts are expected with a couple of stronger ones in the mountains. This will favor the first half of Saturday and taper off through the day, as the tornado threat increases.   SPIN-UP TORNADOES: I expect to see a number of them, starting Saturday morning and lasting into the late afternoon and evening. Make sure you have a way to receive alerts starting overnight tonight. The most reliable way is a weather radio. You should never rely on outdoor warning sirens. As I mentioned above, most of the time when we talk about tropical tornadoes, they are weak and short-lived. But, we *cannot* make that promise this time. One or two strong tornadoes could be in the picture.   FLASH FLOODING: There is an area from metro Atlanta into eastern Georgia that I am concerned about. Please see the red outlined and shaded areas on the map, somewhere in there we could see up to 8" of rain. Widespread across Metro Atlanta and North Georgia, 1-4".   RIVER/STREAM FLOODING: Watch area creeks and rivers to potentially get into flood stage if a heavier band sets up over its basin. Unfortunately, we can't pinpoint these until its happening. Make sure you're following my page,  Alex Forbes , for updates in the hours ahead. Information can change quickly; look for the latest. Even something that's an hour old could become outdated. I will be in with Chief Meteorologist  Joanne Feldman  starting at 2 AM.
